p: The line names the wise god by a title, Ninshiku. The Nineveh copy writes his later name, Ea.
b: Ninšiku is a title of the god of wisdom and fresh water. The copy here, a tablet from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (siglum P(+)R(+)KB, Neo-Assyrian), writes his name as Ea, the form later Babylonians used. The Plain keeps "Enki" throughout the book, the name the Old Babylonian copies use. The best copy, A from Sippar, is broken from about line 252 to 280, so the opening lines of this chapter come only from the Nineveh fragments and from copy E, another Old Babylonian tablet from Sippar. That is why so many lines here are torn: the scene of the fourteen pieces of clay (3:96-104) runs on into Mami's rules for birth.

p: Šassūrātum, literally "wombs": the fourteen divine midwives who help Mami shape the first people.
b: The Akkadian šassūru means "womb." The poem uses it for the goddesses who help at birth, and for Mami herself. SEAL's editors explain that the word stands for the fourteen divine midwives of Mami's company, and that Mami's own sign was a womb-shaped emblem. The Plain says "birth goddess" every time. The fourteen, seven to shape males and seven to shape females (3:102-104), now become the helpers at every human birth.

t: Clay, oil and the hand of a goddess
p: The torn lines mention clay and oil. Genesis says the LORD God himself shaped the man from dust.
b: Lines 263-264 keep only "clay" and "oil" (or "fat"). SEAL's editors expected a verb for "mix" but say the signs do not allow it. Agrees: Genesis also says the first human was formed from the ground: "Then the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground and blew into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Differs: in Atrahasis a goddess and her team work clay mixed with a slain god's flesh and blood (3:45-58), and the people they make are workers for the gods. In Genesis one God shapes the man with his own hands and breathes his own breath into him, and Job and Isaiah keep that picture: "We are the clay, and you are the one who shaped us" (Isaiah 64:8).

a: She formed the shapes of the people
p: Uṣurāt nišī uṣṣar: a goddess "draws the designs" of humankind, as an architect draws a plan.
b: The noun uṣurtu means a drawing, a plan or a design, and the verb eṣēru means to draw it. Mami lays out the pattern of the human race the way a builder marks out a house. The other Nineveh copy (S+T+) adds her name: "the forms of the people Mami draws." Genesis says something stronger: the pattern of humankind is God himself, "in his image ... male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27).

t: A later scribe rewrites the birth rules
p: Lines 265a-f are found only in the Nineveh copy. They repeat the Old Babylonian rules of 4:36-41 with changes.
b: This little speech is only in the Nineveh copy S+T+, written about a thousand years after the Old Babylonian copies. It is a version of the rules Mami gives again at 4:36-41. SEAL's editors note that the later scribe did not understand two old words: where the Old Babylonian text has the midwife rejoice "in the house of the holy woman" (4:36), he wrote "in the house of the woman in labor," and he replaced the verb for the mother's time apart (4:39) with a verb for being in labor (4:11). Here and in 4:40 the number of days differs too: seven in this copy, nine in the older ones.

a: let the brick be laid down
p: Babylonian women gave birth over bricks. Exodus 1:16 has Pharaoh tell the midwives to watch "the two stones."
b: The brick (libittu) was the place of birth: the mother crouched over it, and Mami laid one down between the fourteen pieces of clay (3:99). Here the brick stays in the house for seven days; the Old Babylonian copies say nine (4:40). The site's note on Exodus 1:16 explains Pharaoh's order to watch "the two stones" the same way, as birth bricks. Leviticus 12:2 also counts seven days after a birth, but for a different purpose: not to honor a goddess, but to mark the mother's time of uncleanness before she comes back to the sanctuary.

p: Dingirmah is a Sumerian title of the mother goddess. "Be honored" is literally "be made heavy."
b: Dingir-maḫ is Sumerian for "exalted deity," another title of Mami, who is also Nintu and Belet-ili. The verb i tuktabbit comes from kabātu, "to be heavy": to honor someone is to give them weight. The same root runs through the poem. The gods' work was "heavy" (1:4); the noise of humankind will grow "too heavy" for Enlil (5:8). Hebrew has the same root: kaved, "heavy," and kavod, "glory." When Genesis 18:20 says Sodom's sin "weighs very heavy," it uses it too.

p: Mami's rule makes every birth a feast for the goddess. Jesus speaks of the mother's joy that a person is born.
b: In the poem the midwife rejoices because a birth honors Mami, who made the first people. The Bible keeps the joy but gives it to the mother and to God: "She is glad that a person has been born into the world" (John 16:21). The Bible's midwives are remembered for a different reason. In Egypt, Shiphrah and Puah would not kill the Hebrew boys: "But the midwives feared God" (Exodus 1:17), and God made households for them (Exodus 1:21).

a: Let the male grow into a young man
p: Mami's words set the pattern of a human life: boy to young man, girl to young woman, then marriage.
b: Lines 266-276 move from birth to growing up. The torn lines 271-274 describe, as SEAL's editors explain, the signs of becoming adult: something on the girl's chest and a beard on the young man's cheek. Then the young people look at each other and choose. Agrees: Genesis also makes humankind male and female from the start (Genesis 1:27) and moves at once to marriage (Genesis 2:24). Differs: here a goddess decrees the pattern so that the workers of the gods will go on being born. In Genesis the man and the woman are a gift to each other, and Jesus reads that verse as God's own joining: "What God has yoked together, then, no human being should separate" (Matthew 19:6).

p: To "lift the eyes to" someone is to notice and desire them. Hebrew uses the same picture.
b: Īnšu liššī, "let him lift his eye," means to look at someone with desire or choice. Hebrew has the same idiom: Potiphar's wife "cast her eyes on Joseph" (Genesis 39:7), literally "lifted her eyes to Joseph." Mami blesses the look that leads to marriage; Genesis 39 shows the same look turning to sin.

p: The Akkadian can mean the young woman gains her charm, or the young man takes it. The Plain follows the grammar.
b: Lilqe ardatum kuzubša: "let take the young woman her charm." Because ardatum is in the subject form, the Plain reads it as the young woman taking on (growing into) her charm, which fits the next lines about the signs of growing up. SEAL's editors translate it the other way, with the young man as the one who takes the young woman's charms. Kuzbu is attractiveness, the word used of a goddess's or a woman's allure.

p: The verb is a precative, "let them choose each other." Other editors read it as a past or a future.
b: Liḫtirū aššatum mussa, "let the wife and her husband choose each other." The first sign is restored. SEAL's editors restore a wish ("let them"), because in their view Mami's speech ends only here; von Soden read a past tense ("they chose"), and Foster a future ("will choose"). "In the orchards" is Wilcke's restoration, which SEAL follows. The picture of young people meeting in orchards and streets is close to the Song of Songs, where the young woman goes "through its streets and its open squares" to look for the one she loves (Song of Songs 3:2).

p: Nintu is another name of Mami, the mother goddess. The copies switch between her names.
b: The mother goddess has several names in the poem: Mami, Nintu, Belet-ili ("Lady of the gods") and Dingirmah. The gods have just given her a new title, "Mistress of All the Gods" (3:83). The copies do not always agree which name a line uses: at 4:41 copy A has Nintu where copy E has Belet-ili. The Plain keeps whatever name the line has.

p: Babylonians counted ten lunar months for a pregnancy. In the Bible it is God who knits the child in the womb.
b: Nintu counts the months, and the birth comes in "the tenth month" (4:27). Counting by moons, the nine months of a pregnancy reach into a tenth month. Differs: in Atrahasis the goddesses watch over the count. The Bible gives that care to God himself: "you wove me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13), and "Before I shaped you in the belly, I knew you" (Jeremiah 1:5).

p: Šīmāti, "destinies": a birth is a moment when a fate is fixed.
b: Šīmtu is what is fixed: a fate, a destiny, the will of the gods for a person. Lambert and Millard restored "the time of" before it, as SEAL reports. The idea that birth fixes a fate runs through Babylonian religion, and Mami is "the birth goddess, who shapes destiny" (3:105). The Bible also speaks of days planned before birth, but as the plan of a Father who knows his child (Psalm 139:16).

p: The first word is uncertain. SEAL reads "she peeled off the rods" and compares Jacob's peeled branches.
b: Copy A has iḫ?-lu-up pa-le-e si-li-tam ip-te. The last words are clear: "she opened the silītu," which the Chicago dictionary takes as a poetic word for the womb, while Stol takes it as the birth sac that the midwife breaks. The first two words are unclear. SEAL's editors, following von Soden, read "she peeled off the rods," and they compare Jacob peeling white stripes in branches to make the flocks fertile (Genesis 30:37). The verb is not certain, so the Plain leaves a gap.

p: In the poem a birth goddess opens the womb. In Genesis God opens and closes wombs.
b: Differs: the Bible gives this act to God alone. "The LORD saw that Leah was the unloved one, and he opened her womb" (Genesis 29:31); "God remembered Rachel ... and opened her womb" (Genesis 30:22). He also closes wombs, for a time and for a reason (Genesis 20:18; 1 Samuel 1:5). Isaiah turns it into a promise: "Would I, who bring to birth, shut the womb?" (Isaiah 66:9). The same picture comes back in Tablet II, where Enlil orders the womb tied shut (6:31).

p: The goddess covers her head, ties her belt, blesses, draws with flour and lays down the brick.
b: Lines 283-288 read like a description of what a Babylonian midwife did: she covered her head, girded her waist for the work, spoke a blessing, drew with flour and set down the brick. SEAL's editors translate the flour line as drawing a circle, probably a ritual mark around the place of birth. Ezekiel 16:4 lists what an Israelite midwife did once the baby came: cut the cord, wash it, rub it with salt and wrap it. The Bible forbids the magic of the nations (Deuteronomy 18:10-11) but keeps the plain care.

a: I created! My own hands made it!
p: Mami claims the making of humankind. In the Bible only God says this of people.
b: Anākumi abni īpušā qātāya. The particle -mi marks the words as a saying, perhaps one spoken at every birth. Differs: in the Bible this boast belongs to God: "I am the one who made the earth / and created humankind on it. / My own hands stretched out the heavens" (Isaiah 45:12). The psalmist answers with trust: "Your own hands made me and shaped me" (Psalm 119:73). A goddess who needs the help of a slain god and fourteen helpers is not the Maker of Genesis, who speaks and it is so.

a: the house of the holy woman
p: Qadištu is the Akkadian form of Hebrew qedeshah, the "holy woman" of Genesis 38:21.
b: Bīt qadišti, "the house of the qadištu." The word means "set apart, holy" and is the same word as the Hebrew qedeshah, which the Plain renders "holy woman" at Genesis 38:21 and "shrine woman" at Deuteronomy 23:17. SEAL's editors point to Stol's study of the qadištu in this context: here she is linked with births, and the site's note on Genesis 38:21 says such a woman could serve as a midwife or wet nurse. This line is one reason many scholars now doubt the old translation "temple prostitute" (see the notes at Deuteronomy 23:17 and Hosea 4:14). The later Nineveh scribe replaced the word (4:6).

p: The verb means to separate oneself: the days after birth when the mother stays apart with her baby.
b: Uḫarrû ramanša, from (w)urrû. SEAL's editors, following Stol, take it as the time after birth when the mother is kept apart with her child, not the cutting of the cord, which the midwife does. Leviticus 12 also sets the new mother apart, seven days and then thirty-three: "Then for thirty-three days she is to stay in her blood purifying" (Leviticus 12:4). The site's notes on Leviticus 12:2 give the reasons readers have proposed.

t: Mami and Eve, "mother of everyone living"?
p: Is the mother goddess a memory of Eve? Weighed: unlikely.
b: Mami is honored at every birth as the one who formed humankind, and Genesis calls Eve "the mother of everyone living" (Genesis 3:20). What fits: both stand at the start of human birth, and in both stories birth comes with pain and danger (Genesis 3:16). What does not: Mami is a goddess who shapes people from clay and helps at births; she never bears a child herself in the poem. Eve is a woman made from the man, who bears Cain and Abel. Their roles are different, not the same role remembered two ways. In what I checked, no scholar argues that they are one figure. Verdict: unlikely. The real link is a contrast: Genesis gives the honor of birth to a human mother and to God.

a: the days of being wife and husband
p: Aššūtu u mutūtu: the legal words for being a wife and a husband, in that order, as in Babylonian contracts.
b: The pair aššūtu and mutūtu, "wifehood and husbandhood," comes from everyday legal texts. SEAL's editors note that this order, wife first, is the usual one in such documents. Lines 295a-b come only from the Nineveh copy P(+)R(+)KB; the second line ends with "let Dingirmah be glad." The poem ties marriage to the birth goddess: marriage exists so that children will be born.

p: A wish about Mami, not an order to the gods, as SEAL reads the grammar.
b: Mami ... i tabbi. SEAL's editors read the verb as a wish in the third person, "let her announce," not a command ("call!") as Lambert and Millard and Foster took it. Mami seems to proclaim something about the couple, perhaps their marriage. The object is broken.

t: The reed mat and the bed
p: The bride's bed: a reed mat laid on the floor. The next line speaks of laying the bed.
b: I taddi kītam, "let her lay down the reed mat." SEAL's editors follow von Soden: the verb is nadû, "lay down," and the noun is kītu, a reed mat, which the next line confirms with "laying the bed." Older editions read the verb as "praise" and the noun as the city of Kesh, a center of the mother goddess (see the variant). The Bible honors the marriage bed too: "the marriage bed is to stay unstained" (Hebrews 13:4).

a: For nine days let there be joy.
p: Nine days of joy for a wedding. In the Bible a wedding feast lasts seven days.
b: The Old Babylonian copy sets nine days for the brick (4:40) and nine days of rejoicing for a marriage. Israelite weddings lasted a week: Laban tells Jacob, "Finish this one's wedding week" (Genesis 29:27), and Samson's riddle runs "within the seven days of the feast" (Judges 14:12). Jesus begins his signs at a wedding (John 2:1-11).

p: Ishhara was a goddess of love; here she is made one with Ishtar.
b: Ishtar was the great Mesopotamian goddess of love and war. SEAL's editors note that Ishhara, a goddess of love, was equated with Ishtar, and that the Nineveh copy confirms Lambert and Millard's restoration of the verb, "let them keep calling." The Bible knows Ishtar's world well: the site's topic on the Queen of Heaven says scholars usually identify that goddess, to whom the women of Judah baked cakes (Jeremiah 7:18; 44:17), with Ishtar or Astarte. Solomon went after "Ashtoreth, goddess of the Sidonians" (1 Kings 11:5).

p: About twenty lines are lost, and the next twenty-five survive only in scraps.
b: Copy A keeps only a few signs of lines 308-327. Millard (1967) summed up what the poem seems to tell here: after the making of humankind comes "a short, and damaged, account of how he now laboured on earth." The scraps that follow fit that: a man, a son and his father, people sitting down, someone carrying a wooden tool, and Enlil.

a: (Here the scribe marked a count of the lines: fifty and more.)
p: At the foot of a column the scribe wrote how many lines it held.
b: Copy A has a ruled line and a number at the end of column vi: "50 and more" in the score (SEAL's translation gives 54). The same scribe wrote "56" at the end of the next column (5:53) and gave the total at the end of the tablet: 416 lines (5:86). Counting the lines let a reader check that nothing had been left out of a copy.

p: La ga is read as lagû, slag left in a kiln. The word for the kiln is uncertain.
b: Itaḫzū laga ti-nu?-ri?-im?. SEAL's editors derive la ga from lagû, "slag from a kiln," and take ti- as perhaps the start of tinūru, "oven, kiln"; von Soden proposed other words. If they are right, people are firing clay or metal to make the tools of the next line.

a: they made hoes and spades anew
p: The gods burned their tools in their strike. Now humans make new hoes and spades and dig the dikes.
b: In Tablet I the rebel gods "threw fire on their tools, fire on their spades" (2:28-29). Now the new people make "hoes and spades anew" and build dikes: the work the gods refused is theirs. Agrees: Genesis also gives work to humans from the start: "to work it and to guard it" (Genesis 2:15), and Tubal-cain "hammered out every kind of tool" (Genesis 4:22). Differs: in Atrahasis humans exist for the gods' labor. In Genesis work is a calling in God's garden before it becomes toil under the curse (Genesis 3:17-19), and Jesus calls the worn out to rest: "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).

p: The break probably held "the gods": people now feed both themselves and the gods.
b: Bubūtiš nišī tītiš [...], "for the hunger of the people, for the food of ..." SEAL restores "the gods" in the gap. If that is right, the line states the poem's plan: humans grow the food that the gods eat in their temples. The Flood will later leave the gods hungry (see the note on Genesis 8:21). Differs: the God of the Bible does not need food: "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you, / for the world and everything in it is mine" (Psalm 50:12). Paul told the Athenians the same: "Nor do human hands tend to him, as if he were short of anything" (Acts 17:25). SEAL notes that this word for food is not yet in the dictionaries.

t: Six hundred years, and Noah's six hundredth year
p: Claude's theory: the poem counts in units of 600 years, and Genesis dates the Flood to Noah's 600th year.
b: This is my own observation. Babylonians counted in sixties, and 600 and 3,600 were round units. The poem measures the growth of humankind in 600-year steps: "... six hundred years" here, then "Not yet 1,200 years had passed" at the end of the tablet and the start of the next (5:82; 6:1). SEAL's editors say it is open whether line 352 had 600 or a multiple. Genesis dates the Flood by the same round number: "Noah was 600 years old when the flood came" (Genesis 7:6; compare Genesis 7:11). In Genesis it is the age of one righteous man, not a clock running out on a noisy race. I have not found this link argued in what I checked; Millard (1967) makes a related point about the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 (see 5:82).

a: The land grew wide, and the people grew many.
p: In Atrahasis the growth of humankind is the trouble. In Genesis it is God's blessing.
b: This line opens all three cycles of trouble (here, 6:2, and Tablet II, segment E). Agrees: Genesis also begins the Flood story with growth: "When humankind began to grow many on the face of the ground" (Genesis 6:1). Differs, at the root: in Genesis growth is what God commanded: "Be fruitful and grow many. Fill the earth" (Genesis 1:28), and after the Flood he says it again (Genesis 9:1). What God judges in Genesis is not numbers but evil and violence (Genesis 6:5, 11). Anne Kilmer (1972) and William Moran (1971), as Tikva Frymer-Kensky reports, showed independently that the gods' problem in Atrahasis was overpopulation.

p: Išappu: "was loud, was thick." Enki later uses the same verb for the heralds' noise.
b: The verb šapû means to be thick, dense, loud. The land itself is as loud as a bellowing bull. The same verb comes back in Enki's advice: "let them make the noise roar in the land" (5:39), where the heralds turn noise against Namtar. The Plain uses "roar" both times so the link shows.

p: Ittaḫdar: "became dark, gloomy, troubled." The god is Enlil.
b: Adāru is to be dark, gloomy, worried. "The god" is Enlil, the ruler of the earth, who is named two lines later. The word for the cause is lost in copy A; the Nineveh copy has "their noise," and Tablet II has "their uproar" (6:4). A late Nineveh scribe misread this line: SEAL's editors note that copy Q took "the god" as plural and the verb as "went down" (see the variant at 6:4).

p: Overpopulation, rebellion, sin, or babies crying? Scholars read rigmu in several ways.
b: Rigmu, "noise," and ḫubūru, "uproar," are the key words of the poem's middle. Overpopulation: Anne Kilmer and William Moran argued independently that the noise is the din of too many people, which the gods solve by plague, drought and finally by limiting births (as Frymer-Kensky reports). A disturbance like sin: Millard (1967) granted that "din" is not "violence," but held that "the basic idea of disturbing deity is surely common to both narratives," Atrahasis and Genesis 6, and he cites Finkelstein as seeing an echo of Atrahasis in Genesis 6. Crying babies: Babylonian spells to quiet a crying baby complain that its noise keeps the household god awake, as David Bosworth has shown; Yağmur Heffron (2014) has re-read the "noise" of Atrahasis beside those spells. The rebel gods of Tablet I also made "noise" (2:41). The text never calls human noise a sin.

p: Enlil decides nothing alone: he calls the council of the gods. The Bible also pictures a heavenly court.
b: Enlil, the ruler of the earth, puts his plan before the great gods, as he did when the Igigi rebelled (2:67-70). The line comes from copy bd, a Late Babylonian tablet from Sippar that quotes a few lines of the poem, and from the Nineveh copy. Compared with the Bible: Scripture too pictures God among a heavenly council: "God takes his stand in the assembly of El; / among the gods he passes judgment" (Psalm 82:1; compare 1 Kings 22:19; Job 1:6). But there the council stands before one God who rules it; here the council is where the gods argue and Enlil needs their consent.

a: has grown too heavy for me
p: Iktabta: "has grown heavy." Genesis 18:20 uses the same root for Sodom's sin.
b: Kabātu, "to be heavy" (see 4:8). Enlil feels the noise of humankind as a weight. Genesis uses the same root for the outcry of Sodom: "The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great indeed, and their sin weighs very heavy" (Genesis 18:20). The two are worlds apart. In Genesis what is heavy is sin, and the "outcry" is the cry of its victims, which the LORD comes down to examine (Genesis 18:21). In Atrahasis what is heavy is only noise, and the god wants it silenced so that he can sleep.

a: Their uproar robs me of sleep.
p: Enlil loses sleep over human noise. The God of Israel "does not doze and does not sleep."
b: Ina ḫubūrišina uzamma šitta, "in their uproar I am deprived of sleep." The motif is old: in Enuma Elish the first gods also cannot sleep because of the young gods' noise, as Mrozek and Votto point out. Differs: Israel's guard is not like this: "Look, the one who guards Israel / does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4). Elijah mocked Baal's prophets with the thought that their god might be asleep (1 Kings 18:27). A god who must rest from his people is not the God who is never tired (Isaiah 40:28).

p: Šuruppû: "frost, cold," a sickness of shivering. It leads the list of plagues.
b: Šuruppû is literally "frost," used for a disease of chills and shaking. With it come murṣu "sickness," diʾu, a disease of the head, and the asakku (5:15). The start of the line is lost in copy A; the Nineveh copy and the Late Babylonian copy z begin "Speak, and ..." The Bible's lists of curses name similar sicknesses: "wasting sickness, with fever and swelling" (Deuteronomy 28:22).

t: "Cut off": a play on Namtar's name
p: SEAL reads eṣû, "to cut off," which may play on tar, "to cut," in the name Namtar.
b: The verb is hard. Lambert and Millard first read "let ... diminish," then followed von Soden's "put out of action" (as SEAL reports). SEAL's editors derive it from eṣû, "to slit, cut off," and suggest a pun on the Sumerian element tar, "to cut," in the name Nam-tar. The Late Babylonian copy z replaced the hard word with an easy one, "let it dwindle" (see the variant). Fate cuts off life: the god's name says what he does.

p: Is Namtar the same being as the destroyer of Exodus 12:23? Weighed: unlikely.
b: Namtar's name means "fate" (the noun namtaru, 6:7); here he is the power that brings plague. What fits: the Bible also speaks of a destroying agent in plagues: "He will not let the destroyer come into your houses" (Exodus 12:23), and the angel "who was destroying among the people" (2 Samuel 24:16). What does not: Namtar is a god who must be bribed and shamed; the Bible's destroyer has no will of his own and stops at the LORD's word: "Enough! Now let your hand drop" (2 Samuel 24:16). In what I checked, no scholar identifies them. Verdict: unlikely as the same being. The resemblance is in the job, not the person. Some Christian readers would see in such plague gods the demons of Deuteronomy 32:17 (see 5:71).

p: Asakku is a demon of disease, and also the disease it brings.
b: Asakku is glossed in SEAL as "an evil demon." In the list of plagues it stands beside chills and head sickness, so it is both the demon and the illness. The poem sees no gap between a sickness and the spirit that causes it. Compared with the Bible: Scripture names spiritual causes of some sickness ("whom Satan has kept tied up for eighteen years," Luke 13:16; compare Job 2:7) but puts every power under God, who calls himself "the LORD, your healer" (Exodus 15:26). The spirit world is real in the Bible, but it is not the master.

a: Namtar quickly cut off their noise.
p: The Bible tells of plagues too, but they come from the one God, and they stop at his word.
b: Command and fulfillment use the same words: Enlil speaks (5:13-15), and it happens (5:18-21). Genesis 1 has the same shape ("And so it was"). Israel remembered plagues: the plague after David's census, which stopped at the altar: "The LORD accepted the prayers made for the land, and the plague was held back from Israel" (2 Samuel 24:25), and the plague in the wilderness, held back when Aaron "stood between the dead and the living" (Numbers 16:48). In both, the plague is the LORD's response to sin, and it is ended by atonement and prayer, not by a bribe.

p: Copy A introduces the first human hero with two words. The Nineveh copy names him and calls him a man.
b: U šū, "and he ..." SEAL's editors explain that these words bring in a new character, Atrahasis, and that lines 364-367 give his background: his god and he are close and talk together. The Nineveh copy fills out the line (see the variant): "[the master] of good sense, Atrahasis, the man." SEAL's editors note that "man" here stands against "god": this is the first time a human being takes a part in the story. Compare how Job is introduced: "A man lived in the land of Uz, and his name was Job" (Job 1:1), and Noah: "Noah was a righteous man" (Genesis 6:9).

p: "Ear" in Akkadian also means wisdom. Atrahasis is wise and listens to his god.
b: Uzunšu petât, "his ear is open" (Nineveh copy). The word uznu means both "ear" and "wisdom," and in the Nineveh copy the hero's name is written with the sign GEŠTU, "ear," as SEAL's editors note. Atrahasis is both clever and attentive. The Bible uses the same picture for a prophet who hears God: "the LORD had opened Samuel's ear" (1 Samuel 9:15), and the servant says, "The Lord GOD has opened my ear, / and I did not resist" (Isaiah 50:5).

p: Atrahasis and Enki talk like friends. The Bible says the LORD spoke with Moses as with a companion.
b: Itammu itti ilišu, "he speaks with his god," and his god with him: the present tense means they talk often. SEAL's editors compare the Babylonian poem "Man and His God," where a sufferer weeps to his god "like a friend." Every Babylonian had a personal god who spoke for him among the great gods. Agrees: the Bible also tells of men who walked with God: "Noah walked with God" (Genesis 6:9; compare Genesis 5:24), and "The LORD spoke to Moses face to face, as anyone talks with a close companion" (Exodus 33:11). Differs: Atrahasis has a friend in one god against another; Noah walks with the only God, who both judges and saves.

p: Atram-ḫasīs means "exceedingly wise." Millard suggested "exceedingly devout" as another possible sense.
b: Copy A spells the name Atram-ḫasīs; the Nineveh copy Atar-ḫasīs; the Old Babylonian copy D0 Watram-ḫasīs (6:57). It is a title as much as a name: atram "surpassing," ḫasīs "wise." Millard (1967) argued that the root can also mean devotion and care, so "the exceedingly devout one" is possible, which fits a hero saved by obeying his god. He notes that Gilgamesh XI calls its Flood hero, Utnapishtim, by this name. The Plain writes "Atrahasis," the usual English form.

a: Atrahasis opened his mouth to speak
p: Is Atrahasis a memory of Noah? Weighed: very likely the same remembered man.
b: What fits: both are the man warned by God (or a god) before the Flood, who builds a boat, saves his household and animals, and offers a sacrifice afterward (Tablet III; Genesis 6-8). Millard (1967) wrote that "the two accounts undoubtedly describe the same Flood" and that Genesis is the more probable account; Babylonians, he said, "could only conceive of the event in their own polytheistic language." What does not: the names, the cities and the reasons differ, and Atrahasis is saved as a god's favorite, not for righteousness. Critical scholars who think Genesis reworked the Babylonian story see the same figure behind both, but as a hero of legend. Verdict: very likely, on any reading: the same remembered survivor of the Flood, told two ways.

p: Only Enki listens to humankind's groans. In Exodus God hears the groaning of the oppressed and acts.
b: Uttazzama tenīšēti, "humankind groans, complains." Lines 369a-d are only in the Nineveh copy. Agrees: the Bible also gives voice to suffering people: "God heard their groans. God remembered his covenant" (Exodus 2:24), and "all of creation groans as one and is in labor as one" (Romans 8:22). Differs: here humankind's god is split in two: the god who sends the plague (Enlil) is not the god who listens (Enki). In the Bible the God who judges is the God who hears and saves.

p: Karṣī akālu, "to eat someone's pieces," means to accuse. Daniel 3:8 uses the same idiom in Aramaic.
b: [Karṣ]īkunuma ekal mātu: literally "the land eats your pieces." SEAL's editors explain the idiom as accusing someone before a third party, and restore it after Wilcke; Foster had restored a word for "disease." The people complain about the gods, Atrahasis reports it to Enki, and, SEAL notes, Enki returns the favor by warning him of the Flood. Biblical Aramaic has the same idiom: the Chaldeans "slandered the Jews" (Daniel 3:8), literally "ate their pieces" (akalu qartsehon; compare Daniel 6:24).

t: "They made us, and loaded us with sickness"
p: The people's complaint: the gods made them only to burden them. Genesis says God made all things very good.
b: The people's words, quoted by Atrahasis (the particle -mi marks a quotation, SEAL notes), sum up the poem's view of human life: made to carry the gods' work, then struck down when they grow too many. Differs: in Genesis God looks at what he made, "and there it was, very good" (Genesis 1:31). Sickness and death come in after sin (Genesis 3), and God names himself the healer: "he heals every sickness you have" (Psalm 103:3).

p: Ardu means slave or servant. Atrahasis serves Enki, as Moses and Job are "my servant" to the LORD.
b: Copy A has ardišu, "his servant" (SEAL corrects a miswritten sign, following Wilcke); the Nineveh copy names Atrahasis. Millard (1967) stressed that Atrahasis is called Enki's "servant," a special devotee of that god. The Bible gives the same title to the LORD's faithful ones: "Have you set your mind on my servant Job?" (Job 1:8).

a: When the time is right, the elders:
p: The words of 374-375 are difficult. SEAL reads simānī, "at the right time," and a cautious "gather."
b: Šībūti simānī / puḫḫir? aqereb bītiška. SEAL's editors read simānī as an adverb, "at the proper time," with Lambert and Millard and against von Soden, and they suggest the verb "gather" with caution, because the signs are unclear. The same words come back word for word at 5:52 and in Tablet II. The elders are the senior men of the town, like the elders at Bethlehem's gate (Ruth 4:2).

p: Enki's plan is spread by town criers. Jonah's Nineveh and Noah the "herald of righteousness" come to mind.
b: Lissû nāgirū, "let the heralds shout." A Babylonian town announced public orders by criers. Compare: in Nineveh, the king "had a proclamation made" for a fast after Jonah preached (Jonah 3:7), and the city hoped that "God may turn back and change his mind" (Jonah 3:9). 2 Peter calls Noah "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5). Differs: Atrahasis's heralds tell people to stop worshiping their gods and bribe one god; Nineveh's herald calls for repentance before the true God, and Noah's preaching is about righteousness.

p: Rigma lišeppû: the same "noise" that annoyed Enlil, and the same verb as the land's roaring.
b: Enki's answer is ironic: humankind should make more noise, not less, but aimed at one god. Rigmu is the word for the noise that troubled Enlil (5:5, 5:8), and šapû is the verb used of the land that "roared like a bull" (5:3). SEAL's editors note that the Nineveh copy has the Assyrian form of the verb.

p: Enki tells the people to stop worshiping every god but one, for a time, to win a favor. The Bible asks something else.
b: Palāḫu is "to fear, revere," the Akkadian word for piety (compare "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins," Proverbs 1:7). "Your gods" and "your goddess" are the personal gods each family served. Enki's plan is a strike in heaven: all worship goes to Namtar, so that he feels obliged and ends the plague. Differs: the Bible commands worship of one God always, out of love, not as a tactic: "You must not have any other gods in my presence" (Exodus 20:3); "Love the LORD your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5).

p: Worship was brought to a god's door, his temple gate. The Nineveh copy says instead "keep up his rites."
b: Ši'ā bābšu, "seek his door." A god lived in his temple, and offerings were carried to its door. Later, the elders build Namtar a "house" in their city (5:66). The Nineveh copy has a different line here: "keep up his rites" (see the variant; SEAL's editors note its Assyrian verb form).

p: Epītu, a baked loaf, and maṣḫatu, a flour offering. Israel's law also has offerings of fine flour and baked loaves.
b: Epītu is a baked loaf (the Nineveh copy says simply "bread"), and maṣḫatu a flour offering (5:44). Compare: Israel's grain offering was "fine flour" (Leviticus 2:1) or "round loaves without yeast mixed with oil" (Leviticus 2:4). Jeremiah condemns the women of Judah "kneading dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven" (Jeremiah 7:18). Differs: Israel's offerings were gifts to a God who needs nothing (Psalm 50:12), not food to win over a hungry god.

p: Libāšma: "let him be ashamed." The gifts leave the god feeling he owes the people.
b: Libāšma ina katrê, "let him be ashamed at the gifts." Katrû is a greeting gift, the present one brings to a great man. SEAL's editors explain the shame as a feeling of obligation: given gifts by everyone, Namtar cannot keep striking them. The gods of the poem can be handled this way. The Bible says plainly that the LORD cannot: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17).

t: Wiping his hand: accepting the gift
p: A gesture of acceptance, as SEAL reads it. Lambert and Millard read "lift his hand," that is, end the plague.
b: Lišakkil qāssu. SEAL's editors derive the verb from šukkulu, "to wipe," with von Soden, and explain it as passing one's hand over the gift, a sign of accepting it. Lambert and Millard derived it from šaqālu and read "lift his hand," that is, take his hand off the people. The Nineveh copy has "put his hand" (see the variant). Either way, the gift turns the god. The Philistines did the same when the ark brought plague on them: "give honor to the God of Israel. Maybe he will make his hand lighter on you" (1 Samuel 6:5).

p: Atrahasis does exactly what his god says. So does Noah: "He did everything just as God commanded him."
b: Ilqe tērtam, "he took the instruction." The poem's hero is saved by listening to his god, here and in the Flood. Genesis praises Noah the same way: "Noah did this. He did everything just as God commanded him" (Genesis 6:22), and Hebrews calls it faith (Hebrews 11:7).

a: He gathered the elders at his door.
t: A man who can call the elders
p: Atrahasis has the standing to gather the town's leaders. Other traditions make him a king or a priest.
b: Millard (1967) pointed out that only a man of high rank could summon the elders. He linked this with the Babylonian tradition that the Flood hero was a king (the list of kings before the Flood) and with the Sumerian Flood Story, where the hero is a priest-king. Genesis gives Noah no title; it calls him "a righteous man" (Genesis 6:9).

a: (Here the scribe marked a count of the lines: fifty-six.)
p: The count falls in the middle of a speech, because it marks the end of a column on the clay.
b: The scribe of copy A wrote "56" at the foot of column vii (SEAL's line 389a), right in the middle of Atrahasis's words to the elders. The count belongs to the tablet, not to the story; the Plain keeps it where it stands, as SEAL does.

t: A temple to the plague god
p: The elders build Namtar a house in their city. David built an altar, and the plague stopped.
b: Ibnû bīssu, "they built his house." Akkadian bītu, like Hebrew bayit, is the usual word for a temple: the god's house. Compare: when plague struck Israel, David bought a threshing floor and built an altar, "and the plague was held back from Israel" (2 Samuel 24:25). Differs: David's offering was repentance for his own sin (2 Samuel 24:10, 17) before the God who had sent the plague; the elders' house is a way to make a lesser god feel indebted.

p: Christians read the gods of the nations as nothing, as demons, or as fallen members of God's council.
b: Christians who meet Namtar in this poem read him in three ways. Nothing: the idols are "something human hands have made" (Psalm 115:4); Isaiah mocks those who shape idols (Isaiah 44:9). On this reading the plague was a plague, and the gifts went to no one. Demons: Moses says Israel "offered sacrifices to demons, not to God" (Deuteronomy 32:17), and Paul writes, "what they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons" (1 Corinthians 10:20). On this reading a real evil spirit received the worship. Fallen powers: readers of the divine council passages (Psalm 82) see the gods of the nations as rebellious heavenly beings; see the site's topic on the divine council. The Bible itself allows the first two together: the idol is nothing, but what stands behind it is not harmless (1 Corinthians 10:19-20).

a: and he wiped his hand across them.
p: The bribe works, and the plague ends. In the Bible plagues end through prayer and atonement.
b: In Atrahasis the plague stops because Namtar accepts the gifts. In the Bible the end of a plague is the LORD's mercy answering repentance: "If I lock the sky shut and no rain falls ... or if I send deadly disease among my people, and my people ... humble themselves and pray ... I myself will hear from the heavens" (2 Chronicles 7:13-14).

p: A Late Babylonian tablet from Sippar quotes this line with Namtar's name.
b: Copy A has "[...] left them." The name comes from copy bd, a Late Babylonian tablet from Sippar that, SEAL says, quotes only a few lines of the poem (I 356a, 412; II A 4, 10). It shows that scribes a thousand years after Ipiq-Aya still knew and excerpted these lines, perhaps for study. See the variant.

a: Their days of well-being came back.
p: Health returns because a god was bought off. Hosea: "he tore us apart, and he will heal us."
b: SEAL restores the line from Tablet II, following Wilcke. Differs: in the Bible the God who strikes is the God who heals, and the way back is to turn to him: "Come, let us turn back to the LORD, / for it was he who tore us apart, and he will heal us" (Hosea 6:1).

a: Their noise became what it had been before.
p: The plague ends and nothing has changed. Amos lists God's plagues with the refrain "yet you did not turn back to me."
b: Plague, relief, and the same noise again: the poem's middle runs in cycles (plague here, drought in 6, famine in Tablet II). The cycles go nowhere, because there is nothing for humankind to repent of; the gods simply want fewer people. Compare: Amos lists famine, drought, blight and plague, each sent by the LORD, each ending with "yet you did not turn back to me, / declares the LORD" (Amos 4:6, 8, 9, 10, 11). There the cycles have a goal: they are calls to return (Amos 4:12), and Solomon's prayer asks God to hear when Israel turns (1 Kings 8:35-37).

p: Some have compared the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 with the poem's 1,200 years. Millard weighed it.
b: The tablet ends with the first line of the next cycle, which Tablet II repeats as its first line (6:1), a "catch-line" that tells the reader which tablet comes next. Millard (1967) noted the suggestion, made by Heidel and Kline, that the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 ("Their days will be 120 years") match the time between the plagues in Atrahasis, and said the number "could have Babylonian undertones from the sexagesimal system." He also noted that Childs read the 120 years as the limit of a human life, not a time of grace. The Plain of Genesis leaves both readings open.

p: Babylonian poems were named by their first line. This one is "When the gods were man."
b: The colophon names the work by its first words, inūma ilū awīlum (1:1). The note at 1:1 gives the readings of that hard line. Scholars call the poem by its hero's name, Atrahasis. The Hebrew Bible names its first books the same way, by an opening word: Bereshit, "In the beginning," for Genesis.

p: The scribe of the best copy gives his name, his rank and the date. Millard puts the copy about 1630 BC.
b: The colophon names the copyist Ipiq-Aya (or Ipqu-Aya; SEAL cites Wilcke and van Koppen), a "junior scribe" (dub-sar tur), and dates the tablet to the 21st of Nisan in a year of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon. SEAL identifies it as his twelfth year and notes that none of the known forms of that year's name matches this one exactly. The same scribe wrote the colophon of Tablet II, copy B. Millard (1967) dated the copy "about 1630 BC." The first readers we can name are thus a young scribe at Sippar and the teachers and pupils of his school.

t: Years named for the king's deeds
p: Babylonian years were named after something the king did, here the dedication of two statues.
b: Kings of Babylon named each year after a deed of the year before: a canal dug, a wall built, a statue set up in a temple. This year name records two statues of Ammi-saduqa, one carrying a young goat to its chest as an offering and one raising a hand in blessing. Hebrew history dates events by kings' reigns instead: "in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes" (Nehemiah 2:1).

p: The second tablet opens with the line that closed the first, and the whole cycle of growth and noise repeats.
b: SEAL's editors list this line as a parallel of I 352 and 416 (5:1; 5:82), and lines 6:2-10 repeat 5:2-10 almost word for word; the Plain renders them the same. The Old Babylonian copies here are B (from Sippar, now at Yale, MLC 1889) and D (in Istanbul, published by Lambert and Millard); the Nineveh copies Q and S+T+ help fill gaps. Repeating a passage word for word is how Akkadian poetry tells that history repeats, as Genesis repeats "Evening came, and morning came."

t: "Did you lay a doom on them?"
p: Namtarra-mê: a rhetorical question. The word for "doom" is namtaru, the name of the plague god.
b: These two lines (6:7-8) are only in the Nineveh copy S+T+. SEAL's editors read namtarra-mê taškunāšināti as a rhetorical question marked by -mê, not a negative command as Lambert and Foster read it. Namtaru means "fate, doom," and it is also the name of the god Namtar who brought the plague (5:13). So Enlil is saying, perhaps with a pun: "Did you not set Namtar on them? And still they grow!" The pun is my reading; SEAL notes the question, not the play on the name.

p: Claude's theory: Exodus 1 reads like Atrahasis turned around: a ruler afraid of a growing people, labor and midwives.
b: This is my own comparison. Enlil complains, "The people have not grown fewer; they are more than before!" Pharaoh says, "the Israelite people have grown bigger and stronger than we are" (Exodus 1:9), and the narrator answers, "however hard they pressed them down, that much more they multiplied" (Exodus 1:12). Both rulers use heavy labor, then a plan against births, and both fail. In Exodus the midwives defy the king, "But the midwives feared God" (Exodus 1:17), and growth is the fruit of God's blessing (Exodus 1:7; Genesis 1:28). I have not seen this comparison argued in the sources I checked; it rests only on the shared pattern.

p: Enlil starves the people to cut their numbers. In the Bible God is the one who feeds every creature.
b: Pursā ana nišī tīʾtam, "cut off food for the people" (the verb is plural: Enlil orders the gods). Differs: the Bible's God is praised as the giver of food: "you hand them their food when it is time" (Psalm 145:15), and Paul told pagan Lycaonians that God "kept doing good: giving you rains from the sky and seasons that bear fruit" (Acts 14:17). He does withhold rain and food as a covenant warning (Deuteronomy 11:17; Amos 4:6-7), but to bring his people back, never to make them fewer.

t: Adad, the storm god, and Elijah
p: Adad is the Babylonian storm god, the Hadad of Syria. The Bible's drought stories show that the LORD gives rain.
b: Adad sends rain and thunder. In Syria and Canaan the same storm god was called Hadad, and the site's topic on Baal lists Hadad among Baal's names. Compare: Elijah's drought is a contest with the storm god: "these coming years will have no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1), and the rain returns when the LORD answers on Mount Carmel. James says, "He prayed earnestly for no rain ... He prayed once more, and the sky sent down rain" (James 5:17-18). In Atrahasis the storm god holds back rain at Enlil's order; in Kings the LORD shows that rain was never Baal's to give.

p: Lišakkil: the dictionaries disagree on the verb. The Nineveh copy has "make scarce."
b: SEAL's editors note that one dictionary (AHw) takes lišakkil from šakālu and the other (CAD) from šaqālu, and that it is a different verb from "wipe" in 5:47. The Nineveh copy has a clearer word, lušaqqir, "let him make scarce," and adds "above" (see the variant). The sense is clear either way: the rain stops.

p: Naqbu, the underground springs. In Genesis the springs of the deep burst open for the Flood, and close after it.
b: Mīlu ina naqbi, "the high water from the springs." Mīlu is the yearly rise of the rivers that watered the fields; naqbu the springs and waters under the ground. Enlil wants both rain from above and water from below stopped. Genesis uses the same pair for the Flood: "all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11), and at its end "The springs of the deep and the windows of the sky were shut" (Genesis 8:2). Here the same sources of life are shut to starve the people.

p: Clouds gather but bring no rain. The covenant curses also picture a bronze sky.
b: Clouds without rain are the cruelest drought. The covenant curses use the picture of a hard sky: "The sky above you will turn to bronze, and the ground below you to iron" (Deuteronomy 28:23; compare Leviticus 26:19). Haggai saw it fulfilled after the exile: "the heavens over you have held back dew" (Haggai 1:10). In each case the LORD says why, and how it will end.

p: Nisaba is the grain goddess. Her breast stands for the grain that feeds people.
b: SEAL glosses Nisaba as "grain (goddess)": her name stands for grain itself. The grain is her breast, nursing humankind; Enlil orders it shut. The Old Babylonian copies have "shut"; the Nineveh copy "turn away" (6:37 and the variant here). Genesis speaks of "blessings of breasts and womb" (Genesis 49:25), but they are the blessings "by the Almighty, who will bless you," not the gift of a goddess.

p: The verb is uncertain, and the copy has a misplaced line count "10" here.
b: Copy D has lū qutturma, which may mean "let ... be dark (as smoke)," with the first sign uncertain; the subject is lost. SEAL's editors note that the scribe wrote his count "10" against this line when it belonged to the line before. After line 23, they add, some lines may be missing, because the Nineveh copy that carries on (segment B) sometimes skips lines of the older copies.

a: Let the dark fields turn white.
p: Irrigated fields in southern Iraq could turn white with salt. Then nothing would grow.
b: Black, fertile fields turning white is salt rising in the soil, a real danger of irrigation farming in Babylonia. SEAL's editors explain idrānu (6:27) as the salt on saline fields. The Bible knows the same curse: "orchard country into salt land, / because the people living there are evil" (Psalm 107:34), and a land "burned out with sulfur and salt, unsown, growing nothing" (Deuteronomy 29:23).

t: Field and womb under one curse
p: The plain "gives birth" to salt, the earth turns back her womb, and women's wombs are tied shut.
b: The poem speaks of the land in the language of birth: the plain "bears" (ulid) salt instead of grain, the earth turns back her "womb" (6:28), and the curse ends with women's wombs bound (6:31). Agrees: Genesis also ties the ground and childbirth together under one sentence: "in pain you will give birth to children" and "the ground is cursed on your account" (Genesis 3:16-17). Differs: in Genesis the sentence follows a sin and comes with a promise (Genesis 3:15); in Atrahasis it is a policy to make humans fewer.

p: Rēmu means both "womb" and "compassion," like Hebrew rechem and rachamim. The verb also means "rebel."
b: Libbalkat erṣetu rēmša. The verb nabalkutu means to cross over, overturn, or rebel; the earth turns her womb back so that nothing comes out. Rēmu means "womb" and also "compassion," the same pair as Hebrew rechem "womb" and rachamim "compassion" (see the site's term for Lamentations 3:22; 4:10). When the earth's womb is shut, its mercy is shut too.

p: Šū is a crop: "a kind of grain" in one dictionary, "pulse, chickpea(?)" in the other.
b: SEAL's editors note that šū is read by AHw as a kind of grain and by CAD as "pulse, chick-pea(?)." The Plain says "grain." Either way the line means that no food plant grows.

a: Let the womb be tied shut
p: Enlil adds childbirth to the drought. In the Bible God shuts and opens wombs, and his last word is life.
b: Rēmu lū kuṣur-ma ay ušeššer šerra, "let the womb be tied, let it not bring the child out straight." Enlil's goal is plain: fewer people. The poem's end will make it permanent, with women who do not bear and a demon that snatches babies (Tablet III). Differs: the Bible also says "the LORD had closed up every womb in Abimelech's household" (Genesis 20:18), but for a moment and for a reason, and he opens them again (Genesis 20:17). His settled will is the blessing: "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1), and "the fruit of the womb is wages paid" (Psalm 127:3).

a: They cut off the people's food.
p: Lines 6:32-43 repeat the order of 6:11-31 almost word for word, now as what happened.
b: Akkadian poems tell an order and then its carrying out in the same words. The Plain keeps the wording the same so the pattern shows. Genesis 1 has the same shape: God speaks, and "so it was" (Genesis 1:7). One line (6:35) is lost; SEAL notes it matched "the high water was blocked, it did not rise from the deep" in the order. Segment B comes only from the Nineveh copy S+T+.

p: Segment C is one column of an Old Babylonian copy whose place in the poem is not certain.
b: SEAL's editors place column ii of copy I (British Museum 109141) here as "segment C" only tentatively. Its first two lines seem to match 6:18 ("Let the clouds keep gathering") and the lost line 6:35, but they found no parallels for the rest. The Plain leaves the gaps.

p: Segment D comes from one Old Babylonian tablet in the Schøyen Collection, edited by Andrew George.
b: Lines 6:51-61 are only on copy D0 (MS 2950), published by George (2009), and have no parallel in any other copy. SEAL's editors read them as the suffering of people and animals from disease and hunger: blood clotted (the verb is not certain), bellies swollen, minds failing (6:53), animals unable to eat (6:55). George took the belly in 6:52 as Enlil's mind; SEAL takes it as a human body. SEAL also notes that 6:55 means "eat," not "make a sound" as George read.

p: The "noise" that kept Enlil awake is now the sound of crying. The Bible's God hears such voices.
b: Ibakki rigimša, "its noise weeps": the same word rigmu as the noise that troubled Enlil (5:5, 6:9). The poem's irony is bitter: the god has his quiet only when the noise turns to weeping. Differs: in the Bible a cry from earth draws God near, not away: "God heard the boy's voice" (Genesis 21:17); "The LORD has heard the voice of my crying" (Psalm 6:8); "I have heard their outcry" (Exodus 3:7).

p: In 1 Enoch the cries of suffering people rise to heaven and the angels bring their case to the Most High.
b: The Jewish book of 1 Enoch (counted as Scripture by the Ethiopian Orthodox churches) tells the time before the Flood from the human side. When the giants turn on humankind (1 Enoch 7:4), people "cried out, and their voice reached heaven" (1 Enoch 8:4), and the angels say, "The earth, left empty, cries out all the way to the gates of heaven" (1 Enoch 9:2) and ask the Most High to judge. Atrahasis and 1 Enoch both hear human voices before the Flood. In Atrahasis the voices are a nuisance to the gods; in 1 Enoch they are a plea that God answers by judging the wrongdoers and saving Noah (1 Enoch 10).

t: A sage, or a righteous man?
p: Apkallu means sage or expert. The Bible praises Noah not for wisdom but for righteousness and faith.
b: Inūmišu apkallum Watram-ḫasīs: "in those days the sage Atrahasis." This copy spells the name with W- (see 5:26). SEAL's editors point to Fechner (2022) on Atrahasis as an apkallu, a sage. Differs: Genesis never calls Noah wise. It says "Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his generations. Noah walked with God" (Genesis 6:9), and Hebrews praises his faith (Hebrews 11:7). The Babylonian hero survives by cleverness and a friendly god; the biblical one by trusting and obeying the one God.

p: This Old Babylonian copy writes Ea, not Enki. The Plain keeps Enki throughout.
b: Copy D0 has ana Ea bēlišu, "to Ea his lord," though it is an Old Babylonian tablet; most Old Babylonian copies say Enki. The Plain keeps one name for the god (see 4:1). SEAL's editors compare the speech that follows, now lost, with Atrahasis's plea in 5:28-33.
